title: Energy, work and power
subtitle: Energy stores and transfers, conservation, efficiency, work done and power
lede: Topics 3 and 8 share most of their physics — stores, conservation, kinetic and gravitational potential energy, efficiency, dissipation — so they are on one page. Topic 3 (Paper 1) adds insulation and energy resources; Topic 8 (Paper 2) adds work done and power. Use the picker below to see one topic at a time. The non-negotiables are the definitions and single-step calculations that must be automatic; the tricky bits are the multi-step calculations and the explanations where the marks go missing.
howto: Choose Both, Topic 3 or Topic 8 under the heading. Sections shared by both topics show under either.
Start with the non-negotiables. Do not move on from a section until every practice question is green.
Read each explanation, then cover it and say it back. For an equation, write it out with every symbol labelled and its unit.
Do the practice questions before opening the hint or walkthrough. Write every calculation in EWAU layout on paper first, then type the answer to check it.
For "explain" and "state what is meant by" questions, write your answer in full sentences, then compare it with the model answer word by word — the bold words are the ones that score.
Fill in the traffic-light self-check at the end of each section. Anything red or amber is what to revise next.

bands.title: The tricky bits

sections.title: Energy stores and pathways

parts.title: The eight stores
parts.html:
A store is a way of holding energy. Edexcel uses eight of them, and the names matter: write kinetic energy store, not "movement energy".

StoreEnergy is in this store when…Example
Kinetican object is movinga moving car
Gravitational potentialan object is raised above the grounda book on a shelf
Elastic potentialsomething is stretched, squashed or benta stretched spring, a drawn bow
Thermalsomething is hot (its particles move faster)a cup of tea
Chemicalenergy can be released by a chemical reactionfood, fuel, a battery
Nuclearenergy can be released from the nucleus of an atomuranium fuel, the Sun
Electrostaticcharges are separated or pushed togethera charged balloon near a wall
Magneticmagnets or magnetic materials are pulled apart or pushed togethertwo magnets held apart

There is no "light energy", "sound energy" or "electrical energy" store. Light, sound and electricity are pathways — ways energy moves from one store to another.

parts.title: The four pathways
parts.html:
Energy is transferred between stores in one of four ways:

Pathway (how energy is transferred)What is happeningExample
Mechanicallya force does work on an objectpushing a trolley, lifting a box
Electricallya current flows through a componenta battery powering a motor
By heatingenergy moves from a hotter object to a cooler onea kettle element heating water
By radiationenergy is carried by waves (light, sound, infrared)the Sun warming the ground

A full description names the store the energy leaves, the store it ends up in, and the pathway. The sentence to learn: energy is transferred from the chemical store of the battery to the kinetic store of the motor, electrically.

parts.title: Describing a transfer
parts.question: A battery-powered toy car accelerates along the floor. Describe the energy transfer. (2 marks)
steps: Which store does the energy start in? The battery — a chemical store.
Which store does it end up in? The moving car — a kinetic store.
Which pathway? A current flows from the battery to the motor, so the transfer is electrical; the motor then transfers it mechanically to the car.

Answer: Energy is transferred from the chemical store of the battery to the kinetic store of the car, electrically (via the motor). One mark for the store it leaves, one for the store it ends in (June 2018 2H Q3(b), Nov 2020 1H Q2(a)). The pathway word is not a separate mark here — it is the answer when the question asks how the energy was transferred (June 2022 1H Q5(b)(ii): "mechanically / thermally / due to friction"), so give it, but the two stores carry the marks.

questions.text: A stretched catapult is released and fires a stone. Which store is the energy in before release?
questions.explain: The stretched rubber holds energy in its elastic potential store. When it is released, energy is transferred mechanically to the kinetic store of the stone.

questions.text: Which of these is a pathway, not a store?
questions.explain: "By heating" is one of the four pathways. Thermal, nuclear and magnetic are stores.

questions.text: A candle burns and lights a room. Which description is in the form the mark scheme credits?
options: Chemical energy turns into light energy
Energy is transferred from the chemical store of the wax to the thermal store of the surroundings, by heating and by radiation (light)
The candle uses up its energy as light and heat
Heat energy is made from the wax
questions.explain: Name the starting store, the finishing store and the pathway. "Light energy" is not a store ("heat" is allowed for "thermal" in every scheme, but write thermal store), and energy is never "used up" or "made".

questions.text: A ball is thrown straight up. Describe the energy transfer as it rises. (2)
questions.model:
• Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the ball to its gravitational potential store…
  • …mechanically (the force of gravity does work on the ball). Some energy is also transferred to the thermal store of the air by air resistance.
questions.hint: Store it leaves → store it goes to → pathway.

questions.text: State the eight energy stores. (2)
questions.model:
• Kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal…
  • …chemical, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic. (All eight for 2 marks; six or seven for 1.)

questions.text: A kettle boils water. Which pathway transfers energy from the element to the water?
questions.explain: Energy reaches the element electrically; the hot element then transfers energy to the cooler water by heating. The question asks about element → water.

checklist: Name all eight energy stores and give an example of each
Name the four pathways (mechanically, electrically, by heating, by radiation)
Describe an energy change as: energy is transferred from the ___ store of ___ to the ___ store of ___, by ___
sections.blurb: Energy is kept in stores and moved between them along pathways. Every energy answer in the exam is built from these two lists.

sections.title: Conservation of energy and closed systems

parts.title: The law, in the words that score
parts.html:
Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another. That is the whole law; learn it word for word.

Two things follow from it:

  • In a closed system — one where no energy gets in or out — the total energy does not change, however much is moved between stores inside it.
  • In any transfer, energy input = useful energy output + wasted energy. If 100 J goes into a lamp and 5 J comes out as light, 95 J has been wasted (dissipated) — it has not disappeared.

Bare "energy is lost" is a gamble: the June 2024 scheme ignores it "unqualified" (earlier schemes let it through). Never leave it bare — say where it went, and it scores every year: dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings.

parts.title: Finding the wasted energy
parts.question: A motor is supplied with 600 J of energy and lifts a load, giving it 450 J of gravitational potential energy. Calculate the energy wasted, and say where it goes. (3 marks)
steps: Conservation: input = useful + wasted, so wasted = input − useful.
Where it goes: the 150 J is dissipated — transferred by heating (friction in the motor, the current in its wires) to the thermal store of the surroundings.
The total is still 600 J: 450 J in the gravitational store of the load plus 150 J in the thermal store of the surroundings.

questions.text: State the law of conservation of energy. (1)
questions.model: • Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one store to another.

questions.text: A lamp is supplied with 40 J of energy each second and transfers 8 J of it as light. Calculate the energy wasted each second.
questions.hint: Input = useful + wasted.
walkthrough: wasted $= 40 - 8 = 32$ J, transferred by heating to the thermal store of the surroundings.

questions.text: What is meant by a closed system?
options: A system with no moving parts
A system where no energy can enter or leave
A system where energy is used up
questions.explain: A closed system is one where no energy is transferred in or out, so its total energy stays constant.

questions.text: A ball is dropped with 12 J in its gravitational store. Just before it lands it has 10.5 J in its kinetic store. Calculate the energy transferred to the thermal store of the air.
questions.hint: The total is still 12 J; the missing part went to the air by air resistance.
walkthrough: $12 - 10.5 = 1.5$ J has been transferred to the thermal store of the air (and the ball) by the air resistance doing work.

questions.text: A student says "the pendulum stops swinging because its energy has been used up". Explain what is wrong with this statement. (2)
questions.model:
• Energy cannot be destroyed or used up — the total is conserved.
  • The pendulum's energy has been dissipated: transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings (by air resistance and friction at the pivot), where it is spread out and no longer useful.

checklist: State the law of conservation of energy in the mark-scheme words
State what a closed system is and what it means for the total energy
Use "input = useful + wasted" to find a missing energy value
sections.blurb: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It is only ever transferred between stores, so the total before equals the total after.

sections.title: Energy transfer diagrams

parts.title: Reading and drawing one
parts.html:
Rules:

  • The input arrow starts on the left; its width represents the total energy in.
  • Useful output arrows carry straight on to the right; wasted output arrows bend off (down).
  • Widths add up: the output widths together equal the input width, because energy is conserved.
  • Label every arrow with the store or the pathway and the number of joules (or the power in watts).

To draw one: choose a scale (say 1 square = 10 J), draw the input arrow that many squares wide, then split it so each branch has the right number of squares.

parts.title: Numbers from a diagram
parts.question: A Sankey diagram for a kettle shows an input arrow 20 squares wide, a useful arrow (thermal store of the water) 18 squares wide and a wasted arrow 2 squares wide. The input is 2000 J. Find the useful energy, the wasted energy and the efficiency.

questions.text: A Sankey diagram for a lamp has an input arrow 10 squares wide and a useful (light) arrow 2 squares wide. The input is 50 J. Calculate the wasted energy.
questions.hint: Wasted width = $10 - 2 = 8$ squares; 1 square = 5 J.
walkthrough: Wasted $= 8 \times 5 = 40$ J (thermal store of the surroundings).

questions.text: A motor's Sankey diagram shows 300 J in, 120 J to the kinetic store of the load and the rest wasted. Calculate the width of the wasted arrow if the input arrow is 15 squares wide.
questions.hint: Find the wasted energy first, then the scale.

questions.text: In a Sankey diagram, what does the width of an arrow represent?
questions.explain: Width is proportional to energy (or power). The length means nothing.

questions.text: Draw a Sankey diagram for an electric motor supplied with 500 J that transfers 350 J usefully to the gravitational store of a load. Describe what you drew. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row below, any 3 of the 4.

PointForWhat you need to write
1InputAn input arrow labelled 500 J (electrical / total input) on the left.
2UsefulA straight-on arrow labelled 350 J, gravitational potential store of the load.
3WastedA branch bending down labelled 150 J, thermal store of the surroundings (by heating / friction).
4ScaleWidths in proportion 500 : 350 : 150 (e.g. 10 : 7 : 3 squares).
questions.hint: Three arrows, three labels, widths in proportion.

checklist: Read the input, useful and wasted energies from a Sankey diagram, using widths or labels
Draw a Sankey diagram to scale from given energy values
Work out the efficiency from a Sankey diagram
sections.blurb: A Sankey diagram shows an energy transfer as arrows whose width is proportional to the energy. Useful energy goes straight on; wasted energy bends away (usually down).

sections.title: Gravitational potential energy

parts.title: The equation and its traps
parts.html:
$$\Delta GPE = m \times g \times \Delta h$$

SymbolQuantityUnit
$\Delta GPE$change in gravitational potential energyJ
$m$masskg
$g$gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth)N/kg
$\Delta h$change in vertical heightm

The $\Delta$ (delta) means change in. Three things the examiners' reports say cost marks:

  • Height in centimetres. A trolley raised 26 cm is raised 0.26 m. Forgetting this makes the answer 100 times too big — the single most common error on this equation.
  • The wrong height. Use the vertical change in height, not the distance along a slope, and not the height above sea level unless that is the change.
  • Mass in grams. 320 g is 0.32 kg.

$m \times g$ is the weight, so $\Delta GPE = \text{weight} \times \Delta h$ — the work done lifting it.

parts.title: GPE of a lifted mass
parts.question: A 2 kg mass is lifted from the floor onto a shelf 1.5 m high. Calculate the increase in its gravitational potential energy. ($g = 10$ N/kg)

questions.text: A 2.0 kg bag is lifted 1.5 m onto a table. Calculate the change in its GPE. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
questions.hint: $\Delta \text{GPE} = m \times g \times \Delta h$, with h in metres.

questions.text: A 250 g apple falls 12 m from a tree. Calculate the GPE it loses. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
A crane gives a load 1500 J of GPE by lifting it 5.0 m. Calculate the mass of the load. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
questions.hint: Rearrange: $m = \Delta \text{GPE} \div (g \times \Delta h)$.

questions.text: A 60 kg student climbs three stairs, each 20 cm high. Calculate the increase in her GPE. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
questions.hint: Total vertical height = 3 × 0.20 m.

questions.text: A trolley of mass 0.40 kg is lifted onto a runway 26 cm above the bench. Calculate the increase in its GPE. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
questions.hint: 26 cm = 0.26 m. The examiners' report says this conversion was the most common error.

questions.text: A ball rolls 4 m down a slope that drops 1 m vertically. Which height goes into $\Delta \text{GPE} = m g \Delta h$?
questions.explain: Only the vertical change in height counts. The 4 m along the slope is the distance moved, which is a work-done quantity, not a height.

checklist: Select $\Delta \text{GPE} = m \times g \times \Delta h$ from the equation list and say what each symbol is, with units
Use the change in vertical height, in metres
Rearrange for m or Δh
sections.blurb: The energy in an object's gravitational potential store changes when its height changes. It depends on the mass, the gravitational field strength and the change in vertical height.

sections.title: Kinetic energy

parts.title: The equation and its traps
parts.html:
$$KE = \tfrac{1}{2} \times m \times v^{2}$$

SymbolQuantityUnit
$KE$kinetic energyJ
$m$masskg
$v$speedm/s

Calculator order: square the speed, multiply by the mass, halve it. The examiners' reports list the two errors every year: forgetting to square $v$ (the June 2023 scheme gives 1 mark of 2 for that) and forgetting the ½.

Write the equation out before you substitute — "write out the equation to remind yourself of the square for velocity" is the examiners' own advice.

Going backwards: $v^{2} = \dfrac{2 \times KE}{m}$, then square-root. Stopping at $v^{2}$ (54 m/s instead of 7.4 m/s) loses the last mark.

parts.title: KE of a car
parts.question: A car of mass 1200 kg travels at 16 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy. Give your answer in kJ.
steps: Units: kJ — the second mark is the conversion to kJ (June 2023 2H Q8(a)(i): 153.6 or 150 both score; 153 600 "kJ" scores 1)

questions.text: A car of mass 1200 kg travels at 16 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy in joules.
questions.hint: Square 16 first.

questions.text: A cricket ball of mass 160 g is bowled at 30 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
A 35 kg child on a slide has 950 J of kinetic energy at the bottom. Calculate her speed. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
questions.hint: $v^2 = 2 \times \text{KE} \div m$, then square root.
walkthrough: $v = \sqrt{54.3} = 7.37 = 7.4$ m/s (2 s.f.). Writing 54 m/s — forgetting the square root — scores 2 of the 3 marks.

questions.text: A tennis ball of mass 57.5 g leaves a racket at 50 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
A 70 kg cyclist rides at 36 km/h. Calculate his kinetic energy.
questions.hint: 36 km/$h = 10$ m/s. Convert the speed before squaring.

questions.text: A van doubles its speed. What happens to its kinetic energy?
questions.explain: $\text{KE} \propto v^2$. Doubling v multiplies v² by 4. Trebling the speed would give nine times the KE.

checklist: Select $\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ and say what each symbol is, with units
Square the speed before multiplying — and only the speed
Find v from KE: $v^2 = 2\text{KE} \div m$, then take the square root
sections.blurb: The energy in a moving object's kinetic store. The speed is squared, so it matters far more than the mass.

sections.title: Work done = force × distance

parts.title: Work is energy transferred by a force
parts.html:
$$E = F \times d$$

work done (J) = force (N) × distance moved in the direction of the force (m).

Work done is a way of transferring energy mechanically. Push a box 3 m with a 50 N force and you have done $50 \times 3 = 150$ J of work — 150 J has been transferred from your chemical store to the box (its kinetic store, and the thermal store of the floor by friction).

Work done = energy transferred. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves something one metre: $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N m}$.

The distance must be in the direction of the force. Carrying a bag horizontally at constant height does no work against gravity, because the weight acts vertically and the bag does not move vertically. Lifting it does: work = weight × height, which is why $m g \Delta h$ is the GPE equation.

Measuring it: pull the object with a newton meter and read the force; measure the distance moved with a metre rule; multiply.

parts.title: Work done pushing a box
parts.question: A student pushes a box 4.0 m along the floor with a steady force of 50 N. Calculate the work done. (2 marks)

questions.text: A force of 50 N pushes a trolley 4 m. Calculate the work done.
questions.hint: $E = F \times d$.

questions.text: A cyclist does 7440 J of work against a resistive force of 645 N. Calculate the distance moved. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.hint: Rearrange: $d = E \div F$. The 2024 mark scheme gave 11.53 m only 2 of 3 marks — round to 3 s.f.

questions.text: A pulley system does 1800 J of work lifting a load through 1.2 m. Calculate the force on the load.
questions.hint: $F = E \div d$.

questions.text: A 20 kg box is lifted 2.5 m. Calculate the work done against gravity. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
questions.hint: The force needed is the weight, $m \times g$.

questions.text: A brake pad presses on a wheel with a friction force of 400 N while the wheel rim moves 50 cm past it. Calculate the work done by friction.
walkthrough: Units: J — transferred to the thermal store of the brakes

questions.text: Describe how a student could measure the work done in pulling a wooden block across a bench. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1ForcePull the block with a newton meter (force meter) and read the force while it moves steadily.
2DistanceMeasure the distance the block moves with a metre rule.
3CalculateWork done = force × distance (in the direction of the force).
questions.hint: Two measurements with named instruments, then the equation.

questions.text: A waiter carries a tray horizontally across a room at constant height and constant speed. How much work does he do against gravity?
questions.explain: The weight acts vertically and the tray does not move vertically, so no work is done against gravity. (He does a little work against air resistance.)

checklist: State that work done = energy transferred, and that 1 J = 1 N m
Select $E = F \times d$ and use the distance in the direction of the force
Describe how to measure the work done by a force (newton meter and metre rule)
sections.blurb: When a force moves something, it does work, and the work done is the energy transferred. The distance is the distance moved in the direction of the force.

sections.title: Power: the rate of energy transfer

parts.title: Definition and equation
parts.html:
Power is the rate at which energy is transferred (or the rate at which work is done). "Rate" means per second.

$$P = \dfrac{W}{t} \qquad P = \dfrac{E}{t}$$

power (W) = work done (J) ÷ time taken (s), or energy transferred (J) ÷ time taken (s).

One watt is one joule per second: $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J to the water every second. A 60 kg student who climbs a 3 m flight of stairs in 3 s transfers $60 \times 10 \times 3 = 1800$ J in 3 s, a power of 600 W.

Traps: the time must be in seconds (2 minutes is 120 s; 2 hours is 7200 s); kW means $\times 1000$ and MJ means $\times 10^{6}$. When a question gives a mass and asks for the power of someone climbing, the energy is $m g \Delta h$ — the June 2025 report says "a very common error was to use the given value of mass (48 kg) rather than weight".

parts.title: Power of a motor
parts.question: A motor lifts a 20 kg load through 3.0 m in 12 s. Calculate the power of the motor. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
steps: Energy transferred: $\Delta GPE = m g \Delta h = 20 \times 10 \times 3.0 = 600$ J.

questions.text: A kettle transfers 3000 J in 20 s. Calculate its power.
questions.hint: $P = E \div t$.

questions.text: A 2 kW heater runs for 1 minute. Calculate the energy transferred.
questions.hint: 2 kW = 2000 W; 1 minute = 60 s.

questions.text: A 60 kg student runs up a flight of stairs 4 m high in 8 s. Calculate her power. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
questions.hint: Energy = m g Δh = weight × height, then divide by the time.

questions.text: A car battery stores 126 MJ. The charger supplies 17.5 kW. Calculate the time to charge it fully, in hours.
questions.hint: $t = E \div P$ gives seconds; divide by 3600 for hours.
walkthrough: $7200 \div 3600 = 2.0$ h. (The 2023 scheme gave 7.2 — a time-conversion error — one mark of two.)

questions.text: A student of mass 48 kg climbs a flight of stairs 3.0 m high in 3.5 s. Calculate her power. Give your answer to 2 significant figures. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
questions.hint: Use her weight ($48 \times 10 = 480$ N), not her mass, in the energy calculation.

questions.text: What is meant by a power of 500 W?
options: 500 J of energy is transferred every second
questions.explain: Power is the rate of energy transfer: watts are joules per second.

questions.text: Two cranes lift the same load to the same height. Crane A takes 20 s, crane B takes 10 s. Compare the work done and the power of the two cranes. (2)
questions.model:
• The work done is the same for both (same force × same distance).
  • Crane B has twice the power, because it transfers the same energy in half the time (power = work done ÷ time).

checklist: Define power as the rate at which energy is transferred (or work is done)
State that 1 watt = 1 joule per second
Select $P = E \div t$ and use the time in seconds
sections.blurb: Power is how fast energy is transferred — the energy transferred (or work done) each second. A more powerful motor does the same job in less time.

sections.title: Efficiency

parts.title: The equation and the percentage trap
parts.html:
$$\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{useful energy transferred}}{\text{total energy supplied}}$$

The same equation works with power instead of energy. The answer has no unit: it is a fraction (0.6) or a percentage (60%).

The trap, straight from the examiners' reports: a 55% efficient oven is 0.55 in the equation, not 55. The June 2023 scheme gave "0.91 or 0.9" (7% turned into 0.07 and then the answer divided by 100 again — a power-of-ten slip) one mark of two, and the 2022 report says of the wrong answers "the answer was sometimes smaller than the useful energy, which should have prompted a check."

Rearrangements you will need:

  • useful out = efficiency × total in
  • total in = useful out ÷ efficiency — the input is always bigger than the useful output
  • wasted = total in − useful out

parts.title: Efficiency of a motor
parts.question: A motor is supplied with 980 J and gives a load 950 J of gravitational potential energy. Calculate the efficiency of the motor.

questions.text: A motor is supplied with 980 J and transfers 950 J usefully. Calculate its efficiency as a decimal.
questions.hint: Useful ÷ total.

questions.text: A radioisotope generator is 7% efficient and is supplied with 1300 J. Calculate the useful energy output.
A pulley system is 64% efficient. It does 1800 J of useful work on a load. Calculate the total work put in.
questions.hint: total = useful ÷ efficiency; the input must come out bigger than 1800 J.
walkthrough: Units: J (2 s.f., as the data; the June 2023 2H scheme, Q9(a)(ii), accepts 2812.5)

questions.text: A 5000 W engine delivers 3000 W of useful power. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.
questions.hint: Useful power ÷ total power, × 100.

questions.text: An oven is 55% efficient. It transfers 660 kJ usefully to the food. Calculate the total energy supplied, in kJ.
questions.hint: 55% is 0.55 in the equation. Check the answer is bigger than 660 kJ.

questions.text: A student calculates the efficiency of a motor as 1.4. What should they conclude?
options: They have made a mistake: efficiency cannot be more than 1
questions.explain: Useful output can never exceed the input (conservation of energy), so efficiency is at most 1 (100%). Usually the useful and total values have been swapped.

questions.text: State what is meant by the efficiency of a device. (1)
questions.model: • The fraction (or percentage) of the energy supplied that is transferred usefully — useful energy out ÷ total energy in.

checklist: Select the efficiency equation and use useful over total
Give efficiency as a decimal or a percentage (× 100), and use the decimal in calculations
Check: efficiency can never be more than 1 (100%)
sections.blurb: Efficiency is the fraction of the energy supplied that ends up where you wanted it. It is a number between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%) — never more.

sections.title: Dissipation: where the wasted energy goes

parts.title: What dissipated means
parts.html:
When energy is transferred, some of it always goes somewhere you did not want. A motor gets warm; a sliding box heats the floor; a lamp's wires heat up. In every case the energy is transferred by heating to the thermal store of the surroundings. It spreads out among so many particles that it can never be gathered up and used again. That spreading is dissipation.

The spec wording: mechanical processes become wasteful when they cause a rise in temperature, dissipating energy by heating the surroundings. Friction and air resistance are the usual causes — they do work, and the work done ends up as thermal energy.

The mark schemes are strict about the wording. The June 2024 scheme (2H Q9(b)(ii)) ignores unqualified "energy is lost / wasted", "not 100% efficient" and arguments about sound; earlier schemes let "lost" through, so never rely on it. Say which store it goes to and how: energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings by friction. "Sound" is usually ignored — it is tiny and ends up as thermal energy anyway.

parts.title: Explaining a wasteful transfer
parts.question: A ball is dropped and bounces, but each bounce is lower than the last. Explain, in terms of energy, why the ball does not return to its original height. (3 marks)
steps: The ball has less energy: after the bounce its kinetic and gravitational stores hold less than before — that is the first mark (June 2019 2H Q2(b)(iv): "(the ball) has lost energy (1)"); the total is conserved, but the examiner is asking about the ball's share.
Where: some of the ball's energy is transferred to the thermal store of the ball and the floor when it squashes and un-squashes, and to the thermal store of the air by air resistance.
So: less energy is in the kinetic store after each bounce, so less can be transferred to the gravitational store, and the ball rises less. The energy has been dissipated.

questions.text: A toy car is given a push and rolls along the carpet until it stops. Describe the energy transfers as it slows and stops. (2)
questions.model:
• It has been transferred to the thermal store of the carpet, the wheels and the surroundings…
  • …by friction — work is done against friction and the energy is transferred by heating to the surroundings; it has been dissipated, not destroyed.

questions.text: Which statement about a 40% efficient engine scores the mark?
options: 60% of the energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings
The engine makes 40% of its energy
questions.explain: Name the store the wasted energy goes to. "Disappears" and "destroyed" are wrong — energy is conserved — and a bare "lost" is ignored unless you say where to (the surroundings, as thermal energy).

questions.text: Explain why a mechanical process such as a drill cutting wood is wasteful. (2)
questions.model:
• Friction between the drill and the wood raises the temperature of both.
  • Energy is dissipated — transferred by heating to the thermal store of the surroundings — so it is no longer useful.

questions.text: A student's experiment shows that a trolley rolling down a ramp arrives with less kinetic energy than the gravitational potential energy it lost. Give the reason. (1)
questions.model: • Some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings (ramp, wheels, air) by friction and air resistance.
questions.hint: One store and one pathway. "It was lost" does not score.

questions.text: An electric motor runs for an hour and becomes warm. Which pathway transfers energy to the surroundings?
questions.explain: The warm motor transfers energy to the cooler air around it by heating — that is the dissipated part. The energy to the load is the useful part.

checklist: State that wasted energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings
Explain why a mechanical process becomes wasteful when it raises the temperature
Give the pathway (friction, air resistance, heating of wires) in an example
sections.blurb: In every transfer some energy ends up spread out in the surroundings as thermal energy, where it cannot be got back. That is dissipation, and it is why nothing is 100% efficient.

sections.title: Reducing unwanted transfers: lubrication and insulation

parts.title: Three things to be able to say
parts.html:
Lubrication. Oil or grease between two moving surfaces reduces the friction between them, so less work is done against friction and less energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings. More of the input energy stays useful: the efficiency goes up.

Thermal insulation. An insulator is a material with a low thermal conductivity — energy is transferred through it by heating only slowly. Wrapping a hot object (or a house) in insulation reduces the rate at which energy is transferred to the surroundings. It does not stop it; it slows it.

Walls of a building. The rate at which a building cools depends on two things:

  • Thickness of the walls — thicker walls, slower cooling (energy has further to travel).
  • Thermal conductivity of the material — the lower the conductivity, the slower the cooling. Brick with a cavity, or foam, conducts less than solid stone.

The spec word is rate: say "reduces the rate of energy transfer" or "cools more slowly", not "keeps the heat in".

parts.title: Thermal conductivity
parts.html:
Thermal conductivity is a property of a material: how quickly energy is transferred through it by heating when there is a temperature difference across it. Metals have high conductivity (a metal spoon in tea feels hot fast); air, foam, wool and fibreglass have low conductivity, which is why insulation is usually full of trapped air.

A question may give a graph or table of conductivity against something else (density, say) and ask you to describe it. The June 2022 report: "the change in the graph has to be described — is it non-linear, gradient decreases or levels off". Numbers at two points are not a description of a trend.

parts.title: Why insulation works
parts.question: Explain how wrapping a hot water tank in a foam jacket reduces the energy transferred to the surroundings. (2 marks)
steps: Property: The foam has a low thermal conductivity (it contains trapped air, which is a poor conductor).
Effect: So the rate at which energy is transferred by heating from the hot water to the surroundings is reduced — the water stays hot for longer and less energy is wasted.

questions.text: Explain how oiling the axle of a bicycle wheel reduces the energy wasted. (2)
questions.model:
• The oil reduces the friction between the axle and the wheel.
  • So less work is done against friction and less energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings; more of the cyclist's energy stays in the kinetic store.

questions.text: Describe how the thickness of the walls of a house affects its rate of cooling. (1)
questions.model: • The thicker the walls, the slower the rate of cooling (the lower the rate of energy transfer to the outside).

questions.text: Two houses have walls of the same thickness. One is built of stone, the other of a material with a lower thermal conductivity. Explain which house cools more slowly. (2)
questions.model:
• The house with the lower thermal conductivity walls cools more slowly…
  • …because energy is transferred through its walls by heating at a lower rate.

questions.text: Why does a wool jumper keep you warm?
options: Wool and the air trapped in it have a low thermal conductivity, so energy is transferred from your body more slowly
questions.explain: Insulators do not make heat. They reduce the rate of energy transfer from you to the surroundings.

questions.text: A student investigates which of three materials is the best insulator by wrapping each round a beaker of hot water. State two variables that must be kept the same, and where the thermometer must be. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1Control 1Same volume (mass) of water in each beaker.
2Control 2Same starting temperature of the water (or same thickness of insulation; same time interval between readings or same temperature change — June 2022 1H Q2(b)(ii): "unqualified 'same time' is insufficient").
3ThermometerIn the water — so the temperature of the water, not the air, is measured (the June 2022 scheme, Q2(b)(i), gave a separate mark for "thermometer in the water"; a thermometer drawn in the air lost it).

questions.text: A graph of thermal conductivity against density for a foam curves downwards and then levels off. Which is the description the examiner wants?
options: Conductivity is 0.04 at 20 kg/m³ and 0.03 at 40 kg/m³
Conductivity decreases as density increases, but the decrease gets smaller and the graph levels off (non-linear)
Conductivity is inversely proportional to density

Quoting two points is not a description ("unqualified quoted values are insufficient"), and "negative correlation" is ignored. "Inversely proportional" was allowed for the non-linear mark in 2022, but it does not state the direction of change — write both: decreases as density increases, and non-linear / levels off.

sections.blurb: Unwanted transfers can be cut down but never removed. Lubrication deals with friction; thermal insulation deals with heating; a building cools more slowly through thicker walls of lower thermal conductivity.

sections.title: Energy resources

parts.title: The seven sources
parts.html:
A renewable energy source is one that is replaced as fast as it is used, so it will not run out. A non-renewable source is being used faster than it forms, so one day it will run out.

SourceRenewable?How it is usedOne point for, one against
Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas)NoBurned to heat water → steam → turbine → generator; transport fuel; heatingreliable, available on demand / carbon dioxide (climate change), will run out
Nuclear fuel (uranium)NoFission heats water → steam → turbine → generatorno carbon dioxide, huge energy per kg / radioactive waste, expensive to build and decommission
Bio-fuel (wood, crops, waste)YesBurned like a fossil fuel, or made into liquid fuelcarbon-neutral if regrown / land needed for growing it
WindYesWind turns turbine blades connected to a generatorno fuel, no carbon dioxide / unreliable (no wind, no power), visual impact
HydroelectricityYesWater from a dam falls through turbinesreliable, quick to start / floods valleys, few suitable sites
TidesYesTidal water flows through turbines in a barragepredictable / few sites, disturbs habitats
The Sun (solar)YesSolar cells make electricity; solar panels heat waterno fuel, works anywhere sunny / nothing at night, weather-dependent

Most power stations work the same way: something heats water → steam → spins a turbine → turns a generator. Wind, hydro and tidal skip the steam and turn the turbine directly. Solar cells skip the turbine altogether.

parts.title: Describing how a source is used
parts.question: Describe how a fossil fuel is used to generate electricity. (3 marks)
steps: Burn: the fuel (coal, oil or gas) is burned, transferring energy from its chemical store by heating…
Turbine and generator: …which turns a turbine connected to a generator, which produces electricity (energy transferred electrically).

questions.text: Which of these is a non-renewable energy source?
questions.explain: Uranium is not replaced as it is used. Bio-fuel is renewable because the crops can be regrown.

questions.text: State what is meant by a renewable energy source. (1)
questions.model: • A source that is replaced as fast as it is used (will not run out).

questions.text: Describe how a wind turbine generates electricity. (2)
questions.model:
• The wind turns the blades (energy transferred mechanically from the kinetic store of the air).
  • The blades turn a generator, which transfers energy electrically.

questions.text: Which source is renewable AND predictable (available at known times)?
questions.explain: Tides happen twice a day at times known years in advance. Wind and solar depend on the weather; gas is non-renewable.

questions.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using nuclear fuel to generate electricity. (2)
questions.model:
• Advantage: no carbon dioxide emitted during generation (so does not contribute to global warming) / large power output compared with wind or solar / low running costs / reliable.
  • Disadvantage: produces radioactive waste that must be stored for a very long time / expensive to build and decommission / a nuclear accident is possible, so loss of life or contamination of an area (Nov 2020 1H Q8(c): each point with its consequence).

questions.text: Describe how a hydroelectric power station generates electricity. (2)
questions.model:
• Water stored behind a dam (gravitational potential store) falls through pipes…
  • …and turns a turbine connected to a generator.

Name the seven sources on the spec and say which are renewable

You need the facts and the ways each is used; comparing sources on cost or reliability is not on the spec — the one 6-mark "discuss the arguments for and against" set (nuclear power, Nov 2020 1H Q8(c)) is on the Topic 6 page, and its scheme wanted each point with its consequence: no carbon emissions so does not contribute to global warming.

sections.title: Key words: state what is meant by…
equations: \text{\"state what is meant by\" = the definition, word for word}

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
"State what is meant by" asks for the definition. Learn these as sentences, not ideas: the examiner is checking for particular words.

TermWhat to write (mark-scheme form)Not this
Energy storeA way energy is held in a system: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic."a type of energy" — the exam wants the word store
PathwayA way energy is transferred between stores: mechanically, electrically, by heating, by radiation.calling light, sound or electricity a store
Conservation of energyEnergy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transferred from one store to another."energy is always saved"
Closed systemA system where no energy can enter or leave, so the total energy stays the same."a system with a lid"
Work doneThe energy transferred when a force moves an object: work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force."effort" or "how hard you push"
JouleThe unit of energy and of work: the work done when a force of one newton moves something one metre (1 J = 1 N m)."a unit of power"
PowerThe rate at which energy is transferred (or work is done): energy transferred per second."how strong something is"
WattOne joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s)."a unit of energy"
EfficiencyThe fraction (or percentage) of the total energy supplied that is transferred usefully: useful out ÷ total in.quoting a percentage above 100%
DissipatedEnergy that has been spread out into the thermal store of the surroundings, where it is no longer useful."lost" or "used up"
Kinetic energyThe energy an object has because it is moving: $\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$."movement energy"
Gravitational potential energyThe energy an object has because of its height in a gravitational field: $\Delta \text{GPE} = m g \Delta h$."height energy"
Elastic potential energyThe energy stored in an object that has been stretched, squashed or bent."spring energy"
Thermal conductivityA measure of how quickly energy is transferred through a material by heating; low conductivity = good insulator."how hot it gets"
Thermal insulationMaterial of low thermal conductivity used to reduce the rate of energy transfer to the surroundings."something that keeps heat in" (it slows it, it cannot stop it)
LubricationAdding oil or grease between moving surfaces to reduce friction, so less energy is transferred to the thermal store."makes it slippery" with no link to friction and energy
Renewable energy sourceA source that is replaced as fast as it is used, so it will not run out."can be used again"
Non-renewable energy sourceA source that is being used faster than it is replaced, so it will run out."bad for the environment" (that is a different point)

questions.text: State what is meant by the power of a motor. (1)
questions.model: • The rate at which it transfers energy — the energy transferred (or work done) per second.

questions.text: State what is meant by work done. (1)
questions.model: • The energy transferred when a force moves an object (force × distance moved in the direction of the force).

questions.text: State what is meant by the term dissipated. (1)
questions.model: • Energy spread out into the thermal store of the surroundings so that it is no longer useful.

questions.text: State what is meant by a non-renewable energy source. (1)
questions.model: • A source that is being used faster than it is replaced, so it will run out.

questions.text: State the law of conservation of energy. (1)
questions.model: • Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.

options: Light and electricity are pathways, not stores; the answer should name the store the energy ends in (thermal store of the surroundings — "heat" is accepted for thermal) rather than "light energy", which is not a store
questions.explain: Edexcel wants stores and pathways. "Electrical energy" and "light energy" are not stores; every scheme allows "heat" for "thermal", but write thermal store.

questions.text: State what is meant by the efficiency of a kettle. (1)
questions.model: • The fraction of the energy supplied to the kettle that is transferred usefully (to the thermal store of the water).

questions.text: State what is meant by thermal conductivity. (1)
questions.model: • How quickly energy is transferred through a material by heating (a high value means a good conductor).

questions.text: "Energy is transferred mechanically." What does this mean?
options: A force does work on an object
questions.explain: Mechanical transfer is work done by a force. Electrical transfer is a current; heating is a temperature difference; radiation is waves.

Define renewable and non-renewable, closed system and conservation of energy
Use "store" and "pathway" correctly and never say energy is lost or used up

sections.title: Describing energy changes: the five situations
equations: \text{from the } \_\_\_ \text{ store of } \_\_\_ \text{ to the } \_\_\_ \text{ store of } \_\_\_ \text{, by } \_\_\_

parts.title: The sentence and the five situations
parts.html:
Every energy-change answer is this sentence: energy is transferred from the [store] of [object] to the [store] of [object], [pathway]. If some is wasted, add: some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings by [friction / air resistance / heating].

Situation (spec 3.5)Energy is transferred from……to……by
An object projected upwards (or up a slope)kinetic store of the objectgravitational potential store (and thermal store of the air)mechanically — gravity (and air resistance) do work
A moving object hitting an obstaclekinetic store of the objectthermal store of the object and obstacle; elastic potential store if it deforms; a little by sound (radiation)mechanically — the contact force does work
An object accelerated by a constant forcechemical store of the engine / person (or whatever provides the force)kinetic store of the objectmechanically — the force does work
A vehicle slowing downkinetic store of the vehiclethermal store of the brakes, tyres, road and surroundingsmechanically — friction does work, then by heating
Bringing water to the boil in an electric kettle(chemical store of the fuel at the power station →) the kettle elementthermal store of the water (and the kettle and the surroundings)electrically to the element, then by heating to the water

The June 2022 Paper 2 question (Q7(a)(iii), a rover descending to Mars on thrusters and a parachute) asked for the energy changes in terms of the work done by forces. The scheme's eight points: work is done by gravity; work is done by the thrusters; air resistance does work on the parachute; this reduces the kinetic store; the gravitational potential store decreases; chemical energy is transferred from the thrusters; energy is transferred to the thermal store; mechanically. The report: "hardly any candidates talked about work being done against gravity" — the store changes were the marks most students got; the three work done by [named force] lines were the ones they missed. Name the force, then the store.

parts.title: A ball hitting a wall
parts.question: A ball of mass 0.42 kg hits a wall at 12 m/s. Describe the energy transfers when the ball hits the wall. (2 marks)
steps: Starting store: the ball's kinetic store (that is one mark on its own in the June 2023 scheme).
Where it goes: to the elastic potential store of the ball as it squashes, then mostly to the thermal store of the ball, the wall and the surroundings, with a little transferred by radiation as sound.

Answer: Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the ball to the elastic potential store as it deforms and then to the thermal store of the ball and wall (dissipated to the surroundings), mechanically by the contact force and then by heating.

questions.text: A car brakes to a stop at traffic lights. Describe the energy transfers. (2)
questions.model:
• From the kinetic store of the car…
  • …to the thermal store of the brakes (and tyres and road), by friction (mechanically, then dissipated by heating to the surroundings).

questions.text: A rocket engine accelerates a model rocket upwards with a constant force. Describe the energy transfers. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

2To…to the kinetic store of the rocket and its gravitational potential store (as it rises)…
3Pathway…mechanically — the thrust force does work on the rocket; some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings by heating (hot exhaust) and air resistance.

3 marks — one mark per row.

2By heating…and from the element to the thermal store of the water by heating.

questions.text: A rover descends towards the surface of Mars, slowed by its thrusters and a parachute. Describe the energy changes in terms of the work done by forces. (3)

1GravityWork is done by gravity on the rover as it falls.
2ThrustersWork is done by the thrusters on the rover (chemical energy is transferred from the thrusters).
3Air resistanceAir resistance does work on the parachute (and the rover).

Energy is lost as the bob speeds up

questions.text: A ball is thrown straight up and comes back down to the thrower's hand, but more slowly than it left. Describe the energy transfers for the whole flight. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1UpGoing up: from the kinetic store of the ball to its gravitational potential store, mechanically.

sections.blurb: The spec names five situations you must be able to analyse. Each is the same sentence with different words in the gaps. The marks go to the stores, so name them; "energy is lost" only scores when you say where to — the surroundings, as thermal energy.

sections.title: GPE to KE: speeds from heights, heights from speeds

parts.title: The method
parts.html:
A falling object (or one rolling down a slope with no friction) transfers energy from its gravitational potential store to its kinetic store. By conservation of energy:

$$m g \Delta h = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}$$

The mass is on both sides, so it cancels: $g \Delta h = \tfrac{1}{2} v^{2}$. That is why a heavy ball and a light ball dropped together hit the ground at the same speed. Rearranged:

$$v = \sqrt{2 g \Delta h} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \Delta h = \dfrac{v^{2}}{2 g}$$

Two ways to lay it out in the exam, both credited: (1) calculate the GPE in joules, say KE = that, then find $v$; or (2) go straight to $v^{2} = 2 g \Delta h$ (the June 2023 scheme accepted either, and also $v^{2} - u^{2} = 2ax$ from Topic 2, which is the same equation).

The real speed is always less than this. Some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings by friction and air resistance, so the kinetic store gets less than the whole of the GPE. "Reduce friction" is a reason; a question asking how to reduce the gap wants a method — lubricate the wheels, steepen the runway, streamline the trolley (June 2025 report).

parts.title: Speed at the bottom of a drop
parts.question: A trolley of mass 1.6 kg is released from rest at the top of a runway 26 cm above the bench. Calculate the speed you would expect it to have at the bottom. ($g = 10$ N/kg)
steps: Convert: $\Delta h = 26\ \text{cm} = 0.26$ m. (The June 2025 report: not converting this was the most common error.)
Energy: $\Delta GPE = m g \Delta h = 1.6 \times 10 \times 0.26 = 4.16$ J, so $KE = 4.16$ J.
Square root: $v = \sqrt{5.2} = 2.3$ m/s. (Dropping the square root cost a mark.)

walkthrough: $m g \Delta h = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}$, so $v^{2} = 2 g \Delta h = 2 \times 10 \times 5.0 = 100$.

sections.title: Kinetic energy: the traps

parts.title: Four traps, four fixes
parts.html:
TrapWhat happensFix
Not squaring $v$answer far too small (the 2023 scheme: 2.52 J instead of 30 J, one mark of two)write the equation out with the ² before substituting; square first on the calculator
Forgetting the ½answer twice too big (60.5 J instead of 30 J)the ½ is the last thing you do: ÷ 2
Wrong unitsgrams, km/h or kJ give wrong powers of tenconvert before you substitute: $g \div 1000$, km/$h \div 3.6$; give the answer in J then convert if asked
Stopping at $v^{2}$54 m/s instead of 7.4 m/s — loses the last markthe last line is always $v = \sqrt{\ldots}$; sense-check the size

Speed squared. Because $v$ is squared, doubling the speed makes the KE four times bigger; trebling it, nine times. That is why braking distance goes up with $v^{2}$ (the brakes have four times the energy to remove), and why a small increase in speed makes a crash much worse.

Standard form. Answers like 153 600 J are easy to get wrong by a zero. The examiners' advice: "it often helps to put answers in standard form rather than risk writing too many or too few 000s" — $1.5 \times 10^{5}$ J.

sections.title: Work done the hard way

parts.title: Three set-ups
parts.html:
1. Brakes. To stop a moving vehicle the brakes must transfer all of its kinetic energy to the thermal store. The work done by the braking force equals the KE:

$$F \times d = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}$$

Given the KE and the braking force, this gives the braking distance; given the KE and the distance, it gives the force. It is also the proof that braking distance $\propto v^{2}$.

2. Lifting. The force needed to lift something steadily is its weight, $m g$, so the work done lifting it through a height $h$ is $m g h$ — which is the GPE it gains. If a machine is used (a pulley, a ramp), the work the person does is force applied × distance the person pulls, and it is always more than $m g h$: the difference is wasted (friction, stretching the rope, lifting the pulley itself).

3. Ramps. Pushing a box up a ramp: work done = push × distance along the ramp (that is the direction of the force). GPE gained = $m g$ × vertical height. Work done − GPE gained = energy transferred to the thermal store by friction.

The June 2025 Paper 2 report warns about mixing up work done (force × distance moved) and moment (force × perpendicular distance from a pivot) — both are "force × distance" but they are different things, and confusing them capped a 6-mark answer at level 2.

parts.title: Braking distance from work done

sections.title: Power the hard way

parts.title: The chain, and the units
parts.html:
Most power questions are two steps: energy first, then divide by time.

SituationEnergy to findThen
person or motor lifting$E = m g \Delta h$ (weight × height)$P = \dfrac{E}{t}$
something accelerating$E = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}$
force moving something$E = F \times d$

Units that catch people: a kW is 1000 W; a MJ is $10^{6}$ J; minutes × 60 and hours × 3600 for seconds. The June 2023 Paper 2 scheme gave one mark of two for "7.2" when the answer was 2.0 h — a time conversion missed.

Significant figures: "give your answer to 2 significant figures" is a mark. 409.41 W → 410 W, not 409 (that is 3 s.f.) and not 409.4. The June 2025 report: "significant figures were often confused with decimal places".

Measuring your own power (the suggested practical): measure your mass on bathroom scales and find your weight ($m g$); measure the height of a step or flight of stairs with a metre rule; time yourself climbing with a stopwatch; energy = weight × height; power = energy ÷ time. Repeat and average the time.

sections.title: Efficiency the hard way

parts.title: Working backwards, and chaining
parts.html:
$$\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{useful}}{\text{total}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{total} = \dfrac{\text{useful}}{\text{efficiency}}$$

A 27% efficient solar panel that must deliver 2.16 MJ needs $2.16 \div 0.27 = 8.0$ MJ of sunlight. The June 2022 report called this "mathematically challenging for many"; the candidate who scored wrote "0.27 × asked-for input = given output" and solved it.

Two stages: if a power station is 40% efficient and the cables are 90% efficient, the fraction delivered is $0.40 \times 0.90 = 0.36$ — multiply the decimals.

Increasing efficiency (spec 3.12) means reducing the wasted transfer, so the answer is always one of: lubricate moving parts (less friction); insulate (less transfer to surroundings by heating); streamline (less air resistance); use thicker wires / lower-current transmission (less heating of wires); replace a filament lamp with an LED. Say what is wasted, then how you reduce it.

sections.title: Explaining dissipation, insulation and lubrication

parts.title: The answer shape, and the banned phrases
parts.html:
Every one of these answers is: (1) what is wasted → (2) which store it goes to → (3) by which pathway → (4) the consequence.

Example — why is the water's temperature rise less than calculated from the heater's energy? (1) Not all the energy supplied goes to the water; (2) some is transferred to the thermal store of the container and the surroundings; (3) by heating; (4) so less energy is in the water's thermal store and $\Delta\theta = \dfrac{E}{m c}$ is smaller.

The June 2024 scheme for that question (a storage-heater brick, 2H Q9(b)(ii)) ignores unqualified "energy is lost / wasted", "not 100% efficient" and arguments about sound. Any two of its five points scored both marks — not all the energy goes to the brick; not all of it stays there; energy transferred to the heater's parts; energy transferred to the surroundings; or the equation argument "if the energy supplied to the brick is smaller, $\Delta\theta = \Delta Q \div (m c)$ is smaller"; "the brick transfers thermal energy to the surroundings" scored 2 on its own because it names the store, the direction and the pathway.

Insulation answers need the word rate: insulation (low thermal conductivity, trapped air) reduces the rate of energy transfer to the surroundings; it never stops it. If an experiment compares insulators, the one whose water cools least in the same time is the best insulator, because the rate of transfer through it is lowest.

Lubrication answers need the word friction: oil reduces friction between the surfaces, so less work is done against friction, so less energy is transferred to the thermal store, so more of the input is useful (higher efficiency).

parts.question: A student heats a metal block with an electric heater and calculates the expected temperature rise. The measured rise is smaller. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: What is wasted: not all the energy supplied by the heater goes into the block…
Where and how: …some is transferred by heating to the thermal store of the surroundings (the air, the bench, the heater's own casing)…
Consequence: …so the block's thermal store gains less energy than was supplied, and since temperature rise is proportional to the energy gained, the rise is smaller than calculated.

• Not all the GPE lost is transferred to the thermal store of the ball…
  • …some is transferred to the thermal store of the oil and the surroundings (by friction / heating), so the ball's temperature rises less.

2RateSo the rate of energy transfer by heating from the water to the surroundings is reduced.
3ConsequenceLess energy leaves the water's thermal store each second, so its temperature falls more slowly.

  • …by friction in the bearings and by heating in the wires (dissipated), so only 60% reaches the kinetic store of the load.

They are all the same because the time was the same
The 12 °C beaker is best because it is in the middle

questions.text: Explain why a car engine gets hot, in terms of energy. (2)
questions.model:
• Friction between the moving parts does work, transferring energy to the thermal store of the engine; the burning fuel also transfers energy to it by heating.
  • This energy is dissipated — it is not transferred to the kinetic store of the car — which is why the engine's temperature rises (and why engines are oiled and cooled).

2Less wastedSo less energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings, so more useful energy is available for the same input (or less input energy is needed for the same output).
3EfficiencyWrite the equation: efficiency = useful energy transferred ÷ total energy supplied — the useful share is larger, so the efficiency increases (June 2019 2H Q4(c)(ii): stating the equation is the third mark).

sections.title: Energy resources: patterns and trends

parts.title: How to answer a trends question
parts.html:
Describe = say what the numbers do, using them: "coal fell from 40% in 2000 to 2% in 2020, while wind and solar rose from 0% to 30%". A description with no figures from the data is worth less.

Explain = give reasons. The ones examiners accept for the usual trends:

  • Fossil fuel use is falling because burning them releases carbon dioxide (climate change) and other pollution, governments have set targets, and they are non-renewable and will run out.
  • Renewables are rising because the technology has improved and got cheaper (wind turbines, solar cells), and because they produce no carbon dioxide while generating.
  • Gas has replaced coal first because it produces less carbon dioxide per unit of energy and gas power stations are quick to start and stop.
  • Total energy use in the world is rising because the population and the amount of technology per person are rising; in some countries it is falling because appliances are more efficient.

You do not need to compare sources against each other — just read the data and explain the change.

parts.title: Planning a chain
parts.html:
Write down what you know and what you want, then find the equation on the list that contains the thing you want. If it also contains something you do not know, that is the step before. Three chains cover almost every question:

ChainSteps
Kettle$E = P \times t$ → useful $=$ efficiency $\times E$ → (Topic 14) $\Delta\theta = E \div (m c)$

Braking$KE = \tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}$ → $F = KE \div d$ (or $d = KE \div F$)

Estimation. "Estimate" means use sensible rounded values and give one or two significant figures. Values worth knowing: a person's mass about 70 kg; a flight of stairs about 3 m; a step 0.2 m; a kettle 2–3 kW; a car 1000–1500 kg at 13 m/s (30 mph); walking 1.5 m/s. A person climbing stairs in a few seconds has a power of a few hundred watts.

The June 2023 Paper 2 pulley-efficiency plan was marked in levels: Level 3 (5–6) needed at least two methods of obtaining data from correct use of equipment and at least two processing steps, in a coherent order. parts.title: Conservation of energy on a ramp
parts.question: Describe how a student could investigate whether the kinetic energy of a trolley at the bottom of a ramp equals the gravitational potential energy it loses. (6 marks)
steps: Step 1 — variables. I will change the height the trolley is released from and measure its speed at the bottom; the trolley and the ramp stay the same.
Step 2 — equations. GPE lost $= m g \Delta h$; KE gained $= \tfrac{1}{2} m v^{2}$.
Step 3 — change. Release the trolley from rest at five different heights, measured with a metre rule held vertically (the vertical height, not the distance along the ramp).

Step 4 — measure. Measure the trolley's mass with a balance. Measure its speed at the bottom with a light gate: a card of known length on the trolley cuts the beam and the data logger records the time, speed = card length ÷ time.

Step 5 — use the results. For each height calculate the GPE lost and the KE gained and compare them (or plot KE against GPE: a straight line of gradient 1 means energy is conserved; below it, some is dissipated).
Step 6 — accuracy. Release the trolley from rest from the same marked point each time, without pushing it.
Step 7 — repeat. Repeat each height three times and calculate a mean speed.

4MeasureMass with bathroom scales; height of the box with a metre rule; time with a stopwatch; count the step-ups.
5UseTotal height = height × number of step-ups; energy = weight × total height; power = energy ÷ time.
6AccuracyStand fully upright on the box each time (full height); start and stop the watch on the same signal.
7RepeatRepeat and calculate a mean time.

Write a full method for measuring a person's power by step-ups or stairs
